paragraphs: Friend, here's what this passage teaches me: doing wrong to get back at somebody never fixes the hurt. Joab was grieving his brother Asahel, and the text says Joab and his brother Abishai murdered Abner because Abner had killed Asahel (2 Samuel 3:30). Joab pulled Abner aside "as if to speak to him privately," and then stabbed him (2 Samuel 3:27). I think that's what hurt looks like when it won't hand the pain over: it grabs for the knife and calls it justice.

Now look at David, because he does the opposite, and it matters. He says he and his kingdom are "forever guiltless before the LORD concerning the blood of Abner son of Ner" (2 Samuel 3:28). Then he orders Joab and everyone with him to mourn, walks behind the bier himself, and weeps aloud at the tomb (2 Samuel 3:31-32). I think the grief was real, and it wasn't for show. When wrong happens, David doesn't pretend it didn't, and he doesn't shrug it off. He tells the truth about it out loud, in front of everybody.

And then he gets honest about himself, which might be the boldest part. David says, "I am weak this day, though anointed as king, and these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too fierce for me" (2 Samuel 3:39). He doesn't fix it with another strike. He leaves the repaying to the LORD: "May the LORD repay the evildoer according to his evil!" (2 Samuel 3:39). So, baker, when somebody wrongs you and your hands itch to even the score, remember this: you can say "too fierce for me" and hand it to God, and that's not weakness. Friend, I've done my share of hiding in the dark, and I can tell you the LORD sees every bit of it.
